---
title: "Regression models"
---

Suppose lexical decision responses become faster as word frequency increases. A regression model can represent this relation by allowing the response distribution to change with frequency. The response distribution states which response values are possible and how they vary. The regression function states how one or more parameters of that distribution depend on the predictors.

We begin with the conditional mean of a numerical response. [Conditional means](regression-models.qmd) are first represented for groups, then [simple linear regression](simple-linear-regression.qmd) represents the mean as a straight line in one numerical predictor. We next specify a normally distributed response around that line, fit its coefficients, quantify their uncertainty, calculate residuals, and compare observations with the fitted distribution.

Once the one-predictor model is explicit, we add [multiple predictors](multiple-regression.qmd), [categorical predictors](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd), and [interactions](interactions.qmd). Each coefficient is interpreted as a comparison between conditional means under the coding and predictor values used in the model.

## Other response distributions

A straight-line mean with normally distributed residuals is not appropriate for every linguistic response. Binary choices, ordinal judgments, counts, and bounded slider responses have different supports and patterns of variation. [Generalized linear models](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) retain a predictor-dependent mean while changing the response distribution and the function relating that mean to a linear predictor.

The generalized linear model pages treat binary responses, ordinal responses, counts, overdispersed counts, and slider responses separately. The distribution is chosen from the observation process, not from the shape of the histogram alone.

## Repeated units

Linguistic datasets commonly contain repeated speakers, items, verbs, documents, or languages. The [structured data](structured-data.qmd) branch begins by identifying those units. Random intercepts represent stable differences among groups, while random slopes represent group differences in a predictor contrast. Mixed effects models combine these terms with the response distributions introduced earlier.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) separates the linear, generalized linear, and mixed effects branches. Begin with [conditional means](regression-models.qmd).
